links.note: 271 says the five elements laugh within (பூதங்கள் ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்) at the concealed conduct of a deceitful mind; 293 says that after a lie about what one's own heart knows, that heart itself burns one (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). Both place the witness to a hidden fault inside the person; 293 moves it from the body's elements, which only laugh, to the heart, which punishes.

In 271 the five elements laugh within at a hypocrite's hidden conduct; in 1040 the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்) at those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing'. In both a part of the material world is the one that laughs at a human pretence, and Parimelazhagar glosses the laugh in 1040 too as inward (தன்னுள்ளே).

272 asks what a sky-high appearance can do if one's heart sinks into what it itself knows to be a fault (தன்னெஞ்சம் தான்அறி குற்றம்); 293 forbids lying about what one's own heart knows (தன்நெஞ் சறிவது), because that heart will burn one. Both make the person's own knowing heart the judge that outward success cannot get past, once for ascetic show and once for speech.

34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற); 272 says a sky-high appearance (வானுயர் தோற்றம்) does nothing when the heart is in known fault. 272 applies the general rule of 34 to the specific case of the ascetic's appearance.

24 praises the one who guards the five senses with the goad called firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான்); 273 likens one of strengthless nature (வலியில் நிலைமையான்) who takes the form of the strong to a cow grazing in a tiger's skin. Parimelazhagar reads the missing strength in 273 as the power to bring the mind under control, which is what 24 names as the mark of the real renouncer, so 273 shows the outward form of 24 without its substance.

274 condemns hiding in austerity to do what is not austerity (தவமறைந்து அல்லவை செய்தல்), like a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds; 586 defines the good spy as one who takes the guise of renouncers (துறந்தார் படிவத்த ராகி), goes in, examines, and never slips. The same disguise that the book of virtue treats as predation is, in the book of statecraft, a tool of the king's work; the two verses judge it by different standards without either mentioning the other.

274 has the hunter hidden in the bush as the image of evil done under cover of austerity; 828 says a weapon hides even in an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and likewise in his tears. In both a gesture of piety is the cover for harm, once in ascetic life and once in false friendship.

261 gives the form of தவம் as bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை); 274 speaks of doing 'what is not it' (அல்லவை) under cover of தவம் and compares this to a hunter snaring birds. Read together, the hunter simile shows the hypocrite doing the very thing, harm to creatures, whose absence 261 makes the definition of austerity.

275 says the concealed conduct of those who say 'we are free of attachment' brings many harms with the cry எற்றெற்று; 655 says do not do what will make you grieve saying எற்று ('what is this I have done'). The same exclamation of regret marks the test in both, in the renouncer's conduct and in the minister's action; Manakkudavar, however, takes the cry in 275 as other people's, not the doer's.

42 makes the householder the support of those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்கும் ... துணை); 276 says none are more hard-eyed than those who, unrenounced at heart, live by deceiving as if they had renounced (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வார்). Parimelazhagar takes the deceived to be the givers, so the pairing shows what the false renouncer exploits: the duty of support that 42 lays on the householder.

276 ends 'வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்': none are harder than those who live by posing as renouncers. 1198, spoken by the woman in separation, ends with the same words: none in the world are harder than those who go on living without a kind word from the one they love. The shared formula uses வன்கண் in two senses, the cruelty of the deceiver in 276 and the grim endurance of the one left behind in 1198.

277 says the world has people who look outwardly like the red kunri seed but are inwardly black like its tip (புறம் ... அகம்); 824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய ... அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சர்). The same outside/inside split is described for the false ascetic and for the false friend.

706 says the face shows what is strongest in the heart, as crystal shows what is next to it (நெஞ்சம் கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்); 277 says there are people red outside and black inside. 277 limits 706: the face may betray a passing feeling to a skilled reader, but a settled outward appearance can be the opposite of the inside.

277 uses the kunri seed for its two colours, red body and black tip; 965 uses it for its size, saying even those like a hill sink if they do a lowering thing as small as a kunri (குன்றி அனைய). The same seed serves both verses as a figure for a small dark flaw in something that otherwise looks fine, by colour in one and by measure in the other.

278 says many with stain in the mind (மனத்தது மாசாக) bathe like the eminent and go about concealed; 298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truthfulness (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால்). 298 states the principle that explains 278: bathing reaches only the outside, so it can serve as a cover.

34 says the whole of virtue is to be without stain in the mind (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல்) and the rest is noisy show; 278 describes people who keep the stain in the mind (மனத்தது மாசாக) and supply the show by ritual bathing. The shared word மாசு makes 278 the negative case of 34.

279 says the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute is upright, so take people by the nature of their deeds (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்); 505 says one's own deeds are the touchstone of greatness and smallness (கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்). The same rule appears as a test for ascetics in the book of virtue and as a test for choosing officers in the book of statecraft.

279 warns against reading uprightness from shape, with the arrow and lute as examples; 667 says do not scorn on seeing someone's form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), because the great chariot has its small linchpin. One verse guards against being impressed by form and the other against despising it, and both replace form with function.

279 says the arrow, though straight, is cruel, and the lute, though bent, is good; 827 says do not accept the bowing speech of enemies, since the bending of a bow means harm (வில்வணக்கம் தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்). Both draw on archery to show that shape does not tell intent, and between them neither straightness nor bending is a reliable sign: the bent lute is harmless, the bent bow is not.

280 says neither shaving nor growing the hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்); 49 says household life is what is called virtue, and it too is good if it has nothing others blame (பிறன்பழிப்ப தில்லாயின்). Both ways of life are put to the same test, absence of what others rightly blame, and the badge of the way of life is not the test.

34 reduces virtue to a stainless mind and calls all else noisy show; 280 says the ascetic's marks, shaven head or long hair (மழித்தலும் நீட்டலும்), are not needed if blameworthy conduct is dropped. 280 names the specific outward signs that fall under what 34 dismisses.

281 tells one who wants not to be scorned to guard his heart from stealing anything at all (கள்ளாமை காக்க தன் நெஞ்சு); 178 says that what keeps one's wealth from shrinking is not coveting the goods in another's hand (வெஃகாமை ... பிறன்கைப் பொருள்). Each gives restraint toward others' property as the means to something one wants for oneself, standing in 281 and one's own wealth in 178; Parimelazhagar reads 281 differently, as about one esteemed for not despising release.

282 says even thinking in the mind (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும்) of taking another's goods by stealth is wrong; 317 says the highest thing is not to do, with the mind (மனத்தானாம்), anything ill to anyone at any time in any degree. Both place the fault at the level of intention before any act, for theft in one and for harm in general in the other.

282 forbids the thought 'we will steal another's goods by stealth'; 204 forbids plotting another's ruin even in forgetfulness (மறந்தும் பிறன்கேடு சூழற்க), and adds that virtue then plots the plotter's ruin. Both treat the plan against another person (பிறன்) as already the offence; 204 supplies the consequence that 282 leaves unstated.

283 says gain made by stealth perishes beyond measure while seeming to grow (ஆவது போலக் கெடும்); 660 says making wealth by deceit (சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்து) and feeling secure in it is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. The same claim, that wrongly got wealth looks held and is being lost, is made to the renouncer in one book and to the minister in the other.

283 says stolen gain perishes even as it seems to grow; 659 says all that is taken with others' tears leaves with tears, while what comes rightly pays later even if lost (இழப்பினும் பிற்பயக்கும்). 659 adds the other half that 283 lacks: wrong gain that seems to grow is lost, and right gain that seems lost returns.

283 says stolen gain perishes while seeming to increase (ஆவது போல); 479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure perishes while seeming to exist (உளபோல இல்லாகி). Both describe a ruin hidden behind an appearance of prosperity and both tie it to அளவு, measure: 283's gain perishes 'beyond measure' (அளவிறந்து) and 479's spender ignores it.

284 says intense desire for stealing gives undying sorrow at its ripening (விளைவின்கண் வீயா விழுமம்); 177 says do not want gain that comes by coveting, for at its ripening (விளைவயின்) the fruit is hard to make good. Both use the harvest word விளைவு to separate how wrongful taking looks at the start from what it yields, for the renouncer's theft and the householder's coveting.

368 says those without craving have no sorrow, and where craving exists sorrow comes on and on without fail (தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்); 284 says desire hardened in stealing (கன்றிய காதல்) yields sorrow that does not die (வீயா விழுமம்). 284 is the general law of 368 applied to one desire, with the same stress on sorrow that does not end.

284 speaks of காதல் grown in களவு and means desire for stealing, which ends in undying sorrow; in 1092 the man says the small look her eyes steal (கண் களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்) is more than half of love's pleasure. The same word களவு is condemned as theft of goods in the book of virtue and prized as the stolen glance in the book of love, where it is a lover's speech and not a teaching about theft.

285 says a loving nature that has அருள் in view is not found in those who, with goods in view, watch for another's lapse (பொருள்கருதிப் பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்); 176 says one who stands on the path desiring அருள் perishes if, desiring பொருள், he plots wrongs. Both set அருள் against பொருள் taken from others as aims that cannot be held together; 176 says it of the householder, as Parimelazhagar reads it, and 285 of the renouncer.

285 opposes having அருள் in view to having பொருள் in view; 757 says the child அருள், born of அன்பு, is reared by the wealthy foster-mother பொருள். 757 limits how far 285 can be taken: the opposition holds for goods taken from others by watching for their lapses, not for wealth as such, which 757 makes the support of the same அருள் and அன்பு that 285 names.

285 says அருள் with love is not found in one who watches to take another's goods; 251 asks how one who eats another creature's flesh to swell his own can hold to அருள் (எங்ஙனம் ஆளும் அருள்). Both test a claim to அருள் against a practice of taking from another for oneself, property in one case and the body in the other.

286 says those with hardened desire for stealing cannot stand and walk within அளவு (அளவின்கண் நின்றொழுகல் ஆற்றார்); 474 says the one who does not live in accord, does not know his measure (அளவறியான்) and admires himself perishes quickly. On Kalaignar's reading of அளவு in 286 as a limit one lives within, the two apply one idea, conduct kept inside a known measure, to the renouncer and to the king; Parimelazhagar instead takes அளவு in 286 as the reasoned measuring of the soul and its ends, on which reading the link is only verbal.

287 calls stealing a dark knowledge (களவென்னும் காரறி வாண்மை) that is not found in those set on the strength called அளவு; 175 asks what a fine and wide understanding (அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு) comes to if, coveting, one acts senselessly toward everyone. Both deny that cleverness in the service of taking others' goods counts as real understanding.

422 defines understanding as what does not let the mind go wherever it has gone, but turns it from evil toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது அறிவு); 287 grants stealing the name அறிவு only with the qualifier கார், dark. By 422's definition the thief's skill fails as அறிவு, which explains why 287 marks it as darkened.

34 locates virtue in the mind being without stain; 288 says virtue stands in the heart of those who know அளவு just as concealment stands in the heart of those who know stealing (நெஞ்சத்து அறம் ... நெஞ்சில் கரவு). 288 adds to 34 that the heart is occupied either way: what one practises, measure or theft, decides whether virtue or deceit takes up residence there.

289 says those who know nothing but stealing do what is beyond measure and perish right there (அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர்); 479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure seems to exist, then is not, and perishes without trace. Both make ignoring அளவு the cause of ruin, in the renouncer's conduct and in the management of means; Parimelazhagar reads அளவல்ல in 289 as wrong thoughts and not as excess of spending, so the likeness is of pattern, not of subject.

290 says that for those who steal the உயிர்நிலை fails, while for those who do not steal the world of the gods does not fail; 255 says உயிர்நிலை rests in not eating flesh, and that hell will not open its mouth for one who eats it. Both verses hang உயிர்நிலை, the standing of life in the body on Parimelazhagar's gloss, on one abstention and pair it with a fate after death; Manakkudavar reads the word in 290 as release itself.

290 gives the two outcomes of stealing and not stealing: loss of உயிர்நிலை, and the world of the gods (புத்தேள் உலகு) not failing; 121 gives the two outcomes of restraint and its lack: a place among the immortals (அமரருள்) and thick darkness. Each closes or opens its chapter with the same two-sided reward and penalty attached to a single virtue.
